content: Certainly. 1. Early postpartum contact between mothers and their infants, along with breastfeeding promotion, has been shown to influence both the initiation and continuation of breastfeeding practices. 2. The maternity ward system significantly impacts the success of lactation among low-income urban Mexican women. 3. Avoiding the use of bottles during the establishment of breastfeeding in preterm infants is associated with improved breastfeeding outcomes. 4. Cup feeding, as opposed to other forms of supplemental enteral feeding, has been evaluated for its effects on newborns who are unable to fully breastfeed. 5. Non-nutritive sucking has been studied as a method to enhance physiological stability and nutritional outcomes in preterm infants. 6. Avoiding bottles and artificial teats during the establishment of breastfeeding in healthy term infants has been systematically reviewed in randomized controlled trials. 7. Oral stimulation techniques have been explored as a means to promote oral feeding in preterm infants. 8. Restricting pacifier use in term infants has been shown to increase the duration of breastfeeding. 9. The early introduction of additional foods and fluids in healthy, breastfed full-term infants has been systematically reviewed for its effects on breastfeeding. 10. Early administration of cow milk formula has been linked to the development of atopic diseases. 11. Perceived barriers to implementing the Baby-Friendly Initiative in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, have been identified and analyzed. 12. A comparative study of Baby-Friendly Hospitals in military and civilian settings has highlighted differences in breastfeeding support and outcomes. 13. Pacifier use, early weaning, and infant cry/fuss behavior have been examined in a randomized controlled trial to assess their interrelationships. 14. The use of bottles and pacifiers in neonatal nurseries has been evaluated for its impact on successful breastfeeding within the context of the UNICEF/WHO Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative. 15. Recommendations regarding pacifier use and its influence on breastfeeding prevalence have been studied in a controlled trial. 16. Factors affecting exclusive breastfeeding in Poland have been assessed through a cross-sectional survey of population-based samples. 17. Exclusive breastfeeding rates and associated factors in Swiss Baby-Friendly Hospitals have been analyzed. 18. The relationship between pacifier use and shorter breastfeeding duration has been explored to determine causation or correlation. 19. The application of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative to neonatal care has been informed by suggestions from Swedish mothers of very preterm infants. 20. The effects of bottles, cups, and dummies on breastfeeding in preterm infants have been studied in a randomized controlled trial. 21. The impact of cup feeding versus bottle feeding on breastfeeding outcomes in late preterm infants has been evaluated in a randomized controlled study. 22. The effects of cup or bottle feeding on oxygen saturation, weight gain, and breastfeeding in preterm infants have been investigated. 23. Education and training of healthcare staff in breastfeeding knowledge, attitudes, and skills have been systematically reviewed for their effectiveness. 24. Hospital and other influences on breastfeeding uptake and maintenance have been studied to inform infant feeding policy development. 25. The reassessment of Baby-Friendly Hospitals in Brazil has provided insights into their effectiveness and areas for improvement. 26. The implementation of Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative policies in New Zealand public hospitals has been documented. 27. Antenatal group teaching sessions have been shown to positively affect postnatal nipple pain, trauma, and breastfeeding rates. 28. Antenatal training programs have been evaluated for their ability to improve breastfeeding outcomes in a randomized trial. 29. The Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding program in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been assessed for its impact on early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding. 30. Community-based breastfeeding support programs in Victoria, Australia, have been evaluated in a cluster randomized controlled trial. 31. Scaling up breastfeeding programs in complex adaptive systems has been discussed in the context of maternal and child nutrition. 32. Barriers, facilitators, and recommendations for implementing the Baby-Friendly Initiative have been reviewed comprehensively. 33. The expansion of the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding into neonatal intensive care has been guided by expert group recommendations. 34. Equity in breastfeeding practices has been explored to identify future directions for improvement. 35. The use of an equity lens in implementing breastfeeding interventions has been proposed to optimize breastfeeding practices. 36. The WHO guidelines for protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities have been outlined. 37. The GRADE framework has been introduced as a systematic approach to rating the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations in healthcare. 38. The application of GRADE Evidence to Decision frameworks in clinical practice and public health has been detailed. 39. The influence of health visitors’ knowledge and self-efficacy on breastfeeding support has been studied. 40. Counseling on breastfeeding has been assessed for its effectiveness in improving knowledge and skills among healthcare professionals. 41. Process-oriented training in breastfeeding has been shown to alter healthcare professionals’ attitudes toward breastfeeding. 42. Breastfeeding training for healthcare professionals has been linked to institutional changes and improved breastfeeding outcomes. 43. Hospital-based nurses’ perspectives on best practices for breastfeeding initiation have been documented. 44. Longitudinal studies have evaluated the ability of nurses and midwives to promote breastfeeding effectively. 45. Breastfeeding education has been shown to influence nursing staff beliefs, exclusive breastfeeding rates, and compliance with the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative. 46. Qualitative evidence has been used to inform decision-making in health and social interventions, particularly in breastfeeding promotion. 47. The Baby-Friendly Initiative’s impact on breastfeeding support and promotion in Russia has been evaluated. 48. Mothers’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding in Egypt have been assessed. 49. Breastfeeding in preterm infants has been studied within the context of development-centered care in Palestine. 50. Skin-to-skin care has been evaluated for its effects on breastfeeding in a randomized controlled trial in Northern England. 51. Multicultural perspectives on skin-to-skin contact and its implications for birth practices have been explored. 52. The Kangaroo Method in delivery rooms for full-term infants has been studied for its benefits. 53. Skin-to-skin contact after cesarean delivery has been evaluated in an experimental study. 54. Women’s perceptions of skin-to-skin contact after cesarean birth have been the focus of a quality improvement project. 55. Nursing interventions to minimize maternal-infant separation after cesarean birth have been piloted. 56. The long-term effects of extra contact during the first postpartum hour on mother-infant behavior have been studied. 57. The provision of breast milk for preterm infants has been explored in the context of professional care. 58. Breastfeeding concerns and experiences among African American mothers have been documented. 59. The prevalence of breast milk expression and associated factors have been studied. 60. A randomized trial has compared hand expression with breast pumping for mothers of term newborns with poor feeding. 61. The acceptability and feasibility of breast milk expression education and support interventions for mothers of preterm infants have been evaluated. 62. The paradoxical experience of providing mother’s own milk in the NICU has been explored. 63. The lack of privacy for breast milk pumping in NICUs has been identified as a barrier, with mothers often preferring to pump at home.
